sections.heading: Appendix G Broader Impacts
sections.text: This work aims to improve the reliability and interpretability of multimodal benchmark evaluation. By diagnosing whether individual benchmark items rely on redundant, visual-dominant, textual-dominant, or synergistic evidence factors, the proposed method can help benchmark developers identify shortcut-prone or weak items and construct more informative evaluation sets. This may contribute to more faithful assessment of vision-language models and reduce the risk of overestimating cross-modal reasoning ability from aggregate benchmark scores. The work also has potential negative impacts if used improperly. Diagnostic results may be affected by the choice of model pool, the quality of intrinsic structural estimates, and uncertainty in human evidence-sufficiency annotations. If such diagnostics are treated as definitive rather than as supporting evidence, benchmark developers may incorrectly discard useful items or overemphasize particular types of modality dependence. In addition, improving benchmark filtering may indirectly accelerate the development of stronger multimodal systems, which could be misused in downstream applications involving misinformation, surveillance, or biased decision support. To mitigate these risks, we recommend using the proposed diagnosis as an auxiliary auditing tool, reporting uncertainty where possible, and combining automatic diagnosis with human review before making high-stakes benchmark or deployment decisions.

sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The claims in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope. The main methodological claims are supported by Section 3, and the empirical claims are supported by the results in Section 4. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We discuss the limitations of our work in Appendix A. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not include formal theoretical results. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We disclose the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results in Section 4 and also provide an anonymized repository linked in the abstract, which contains the code and relevant datasets. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We provide an anonymized repository linked in the abstract, which contains the code and relevant datasets. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The training and test details are specified in Section 4.1, including the experimental setup, data splits, hyperparameters, and implementation details necessary to understand the reported results. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper reports statistical significance analyses in Appendix F.1. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The compute resources used for the experiments are described in Section 4.1 and Appendix, including the GPU type and relevant computational setup used to run the experiments. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We have reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and confirm that the research conducted in this paper conforms to it. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix G discusses both positive and negative societal impacts. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. • The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. • The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. • If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not release data or models that pose a high risk for misuse. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. • Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. • Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. • We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We use existing public datasets and properly credit their original creators in the references. The licenses and terms of use for these datasets are explicitly reported in Appendix, and our use complies with those terms. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. • The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. • The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL. • The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. • For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. • If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset. • For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. • If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper introduces a new human-labeled diagnostic validation set for item-level multimodal benchmark diagnosis. The dataset will be released through an anonymized GitHub link. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. • Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. • The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. • At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper involves crowdsourced human annotation for constructing the diagnostic validation set. Appendix C provides the annotation protocol. Annotators were asked to answer multiple-choice benchmark items under controlled modality conditions, and no personal or sensitive information was collected. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. • Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. • According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [No] Justification: The paper involves paid human annotation for constructing the diagnostic validation set, but no formal IRB or equivalent institutional review was obtained. The annotation task is minimal-risk: participants only answer multiple-choice benchmark items under controlled modality conditions, and no personal, sensitive, or health-related information is collected. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. • Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. • We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution. • For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review. 16. Declaration of LLM usage Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. Answer: [Yes] Justification: MLLMs are used as diagnostic respondents to collect modality-conditioned response matrices for fitting and evaluating the diagnosis methods. The model pool, prompts, modality conditions, and response normalization procedures are documented in Appendix D. LLMs were additionally used only for language polishing, which did not affect the methodology or scientific claims. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components. • Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.

Item-Level Multimodal Benchmark Diagnosis via Structure-Response Co-Calibration Shiqi Zhang 1 Weixin Zeng 2 Ziheng Zhang 2 Jiuyang Tang 2 Xiang Zhao 2 1 National Key Laboratory of Information Systems Engineering, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China 2 National Key Laboratory of Big Data and Decision, National University of Defense Technology, Changsha, China {zhangshiqi,zengweixin13,zihengzhang20,jiuyang_tang,xiangzhao}@nudt.edu.cn † † thanks: Corresponding author. Abstract Multimodal benchmarks are central to evaluating whether models can reason over information from multiple modalities. However, existing literature has revealed that some benchmarks may contain shortcut items that can be answered from a single modality or from answer-option regularities alone, thus failing to reflect models’ true cross-modal inference ability. Existing methods for assessing benchmarks typically rely either on intrinsic item structure or extrinsic model response behavior , which are not adequate for a comprehensive diagnosis. To fill in this gap, we propose SRCoD, a structure-response co-calibrated diagnosis framework for item-level diagnosis of modality dependence in multimodal benchmarks. SRCoD estimates sample-wise multimodal information structure from benchmark content and target answers, and uses this signal as a soft structural anchor for modality-conditioned item response modeling. The learned model produces a calibrated item-level diagnostic profile that reflects how strongly an item depends on different forms of modality evidence, enabling fine-grained benchmark analysis beyond aggregate accuracy. SRCoD also provides interpretable attribution of the diagnosis results. Extensive experiments under two complementary protocols, i.e., benchmark-refinement oriented validation and human-labeled item validation, demonstrate that SRCoD outperforms state-of-the-art benchmark diagnosis methods. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/Q-17/SRCoD . 1 Introduction Multimodal benchmarks are central to evaluating the cross-modal reasoning ability of vision-language models (VLMs) [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . These benchmarks are in essence collections of items , where each item corresponds to a complete problem instance, usually comprising multimodal inputs, a question, and a ground-truth answer [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Such benchmarks are designed to evaluate whether VLM can understand and reason across modalities [ 9 , 10 ] , and have inspired the development of state-of-the-art VLM models. However, recently, the quality of these benchmarks, especially whether the items are all useful for evaluating models’ cross-modal inference ability, has attracted increasing attention. Early efforts have revealed that existing multimodal benchmarks often contain shortcut items that can be answered from a single modality or from answer-option regularities alone [ 11 , 12 ] . Therefore, item-level multimodal benchmark diagnosis , which aims to identify what modality evidence each item actually requires and whether it provides a valid test of the intended cross-modal reasoning ability of downstream models, has become an important topic. Existing diagnostic methods can be categorized into two groups: methods based on intrinsic item structure and methods based on extrinsic model responses . Intrinsic-structure based methods [ 13 , 14 ] characterize how answer-relevant evidence is distributed across modalities within the item itself, often through information-theoretic decomposition frameworks such as partial information decomposition (PID) [ 15 ] . However, item structure alone cannot reflect how downstream models actually solve the item, as an item may contain cross-modal evidence that models would not use. For example, a sidewalk-color question may contain the necessary visual evidence, yet its question and answer options can strongly favor “gray” even without the image. Extrinsic-response based methods, on the other hand, evaluate the quality of items from model behavior under different modality conditions, using item response theory (IRT) [ 16 ] , multidimensional IRT [ 17 ] , or multimodal variants such as M3IRT [ 18 ] . These methods first select a pool of downstream VLMs, collect their responses to each item under different modality conditions, and evaluate the multimodal benchmark from the resulting response matrix. While this grounds the diagnosis in actual model behavior, it discards the intrinsic structure of items and makes the assessment solely based on the chosen model pool. A narrow or imbalanced pool may yield response matrix that reflect model-specific strengths rather than the evidence an item actually requires. For example, identifying the resting-potential points in an action-potential graph requires both the textual question and the numbered graph. Yet failures by models with limited chart-understanding abilities may not reflect the item’s intrinsic evidence requirements. We therefore argue that reliable multimodal benchmark diagnosis requires a structure-response co-calibrated view . Intrinsic item structure provides a structural signal about what evidence an item contains, while extrinsic model responses provide a behavioral signal about how the item functions in evaluation. We instantiate this view with SRCoD, a S tructure- R esponse Co -calibrated D iagnosis framework for item-level multimodal benchmark diagnosis. SRCoD first derives a structural prior from sample-wise multimodal interaction signals, summarizing how answer-relevant evidence is distributed across modalities within the item. It then uses this prior to anchor a modality-conditioned IRT model fitted to extrinsic model responses under different modality settings. The resulting diagnostic profile therefore provides an attribution-style interpretation of item behavior, with each coordinate corresponding to one evidence factor. In this way, SRCoD preserves the intrinsic structure of the item while correcting it using empirical evaluation behavior. To comprehensively assess item-level multimodal benchmark diagnosis baselines, we use two complementary validation protocols: benchmark-refinement oriented validation and human-labeled item validation . Following prior extrinsic-response work [ 18 ] , we conduct benchmark-refinement oriented validation using model-ranking preservation as the validation criterion. In addition, we introduce human-labeled item validation and construct a diagnostic validation set across ScienceQA [ 4 ] , MMMU [ 5 ] , and SEED-Bench [ 6 ] , which directly verifies whether each method recovers the dominant evidence factor underlying each item. Unlike prior intrinsic-structure work that uses human judgments mainly to assess estimator plausibility [ 14 ] , our protocol collects controlled human labels indicating whether an item can be solved from the visual input alone, the textual input alone, either modality, or only their combination. Across both protocols, SRCoD outperforms intrinsic-structure and extrinsic-response baselines, with ablations confirming the benefits of structure-response co-calibration. In this paper, our contributions are threefold: • We propose a structure-response co-calibrated view for item-level multimodal benchmark diagnosis, and instantiate it with SRCoD, a structure-anchored multimodal IRT framework that combines intrinsic item structure with extrinsic model responses. • SRCoD provides interpretable attribution of the diagnosis results, indicating whether the multimodal features of an item are synergistic, redundant, visual-dominant or textual-dominant. • We validate SRCoD under two complementary protocols, i.e., benchmark-refinement oriented validation and human-labeled item validation . Across both protocols, SRCoD outperforms state-of-the-art evaluation methods. 2 Related Work Intrinsic-structure methods. Intrinsic-structure methods analyze how answer-relevant evidence is distributed across modalities within an item. A representative line of work uses Partial Information Decomposition (PID) [ 15 ] to decompose multimodal information into redundant, unique, and synergistic components. Early PID-based analyses [ 13 , 19 ] typically operate at the dataset-distribution level, while recent sample-wise estimators such as LSMI [ 14 ] make it possible to estimate item-level multimodal interaction structure. On real-world data, these methods often use human judgments to assess the plausibility of estimated interaction signals. However, such judgments are not controlled item-level evidence-sufficiency labels, and therefore do not directly validate whether the inferred modality-dependence profile of each benchmark item is correct. Extrinsic-response methods. Extrinsic-response methods infer benchmark properties from model behavior. A common strategy is to evaluate models under different modality conditions and model the resulting response patterns with Item Response Theory (IRT) [ 16 ] or multidimensional IRT (MIRT) [ 17 ] , treating models as subjects and benchmark examples as items. Recent multimodal extensions further decompose responses into visual, textual, and joint factors [ 18 ] . These methods are often validated through benchmark refinement protocols, such as selecting compact subsets that preserve model rankings or avoid semi-synthetic low-quality items. Such protocols demonstrate downstream validation utility, but they do not provide ground-truth item-level diagnosis labels for naturally occurring benchmark questions. Positioning of this work. Our work addresses both the methodological and evaluation gaps above. SRCoD connects intrinsic item structure and extrinsic model responses through structure-response co-calibration, using structural interaction signals as soft anchors for modality-conditioned IRT and calibrating them with observed model responses. We further introduce a controlled human validation protocol for assessing evidence sufficiency, which provides item-level diagnostic labels for directly validating modality-dependence. 3 Method We develop SRCoD, a structure-anchored multimodal IRT framework that instantiates structure-response co-calibration for item-level multimodal benchmark diagnosis. The intrinsic item structure summarizes how answer-relevant evidence is distributed across modalities within the item itself, while the extrinsic model responses capture how a pool of VLMs behaves under different modality conditions. The resulting modality-dependence profile summarizes four forms of item-level evidence dependence: redundant, visual-dominant, textual-dominant, and synergistic. SRCoD first derives a structural prior from sample-wise multimodal interaction signals, and then uses this prior to anchor a modality-conditioned IRT model fitted to extrinsic model responses. The fitted model produces a response-calibrated modality-dependence profile, which serves as the final diagnostic representation of the item. Since each coordinate corresponds to a distinct evidence factor, the profile also provides an interpretable attribution of item behavior. Figure 1: Overview of SRCoD. SRCoD diagnoses item-level modality dependence by co-calibrating intrinsic item structure and extrinsic model responses. It first derives a structural prior from partial information decomposition, then anchors a modality-conditioned response model fitted to VLM responses under controlled modality conditions. 3.1 Modality-Conditioned Response Model Let 𝒟 = { ( v j , t j , y j ) } j = 1 J \mathcal{D}=\{(v_{j},t_{j},y_{j})\}_{j=1}^{J} denote a multimodal benchmark, where v j v_{j} , t j t_{j} , and y j y_{j} are the visual input, textual input, and ground-truth answer of item j j . For model i i , item j j , and modality condition c = ( c v , c t ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } 2 c=(c_{v},c_{t})\in\{0,1\}^{2} , we observe a binary response r i ​ j ​ c ∈ { 0 , 1 } r_{ijc}\in\{0,1\} , indicating whether the model answers correctly under condition c c . Following modality-conditioned multimodal IRT [ 18 ] , we use four response coordinates corresponding to a base coordinate, a visual coordinate, a textual coordinate, and a joint visual-textual coordinate. For condition c c , the active coordinates are encoded as ϕ ⁡ ( c ) = ( 1 , c v , c t , c v ​ c t ) ⊤ \boldsymbol{\phi}(c)=(1,c_{v},c_{t},c_{v}c_{t})^{\top} . Each model i i has an ability vector 𝜽 i ∈ ℝ 4 \boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{4} , and each item j j has discrimination and difficulty vectors 𝐚 j , 𝐛 j ∈ ℝ 4 \mathbf{a}_{j},\mathbf{b}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{4} . The probability of a correct response is modeled as P i ​ j ​ c = P ⁡ ( r i ​ j ​ c = 1 ) = σ ⁡ ( ϕ ​ ( c ) ⊤ ​ ( 𝐚 j ⊙ 𝜽 i − 𝐛 j ) ) , P_{ijc}=P(r_{ijc}=1)=\sigma\!\left(\boldsymbol{\phi}(c)^{\top}\left(\mathbf{a}_{j}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}-\mathbf{b}_{j}\right)\right), (1) where ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. This likelihood captures how model correctness changes when different modality coordinates are activated. If 𝐚 j \mathbf{a}_{j} and 𝐛 j \mathbf{b}_{j} were learned solely from responses, the resulting diagnosis would be response-only and could be sensitive to the diagnostic model pool. The key distinction of SRCoD is that these item parameters are anchored by intrinsic item structure before being calibrated by extrinsic model responses. 3.2 Prior From Intrinsic Item Structure Response-only diagnosis can conflate modality dependence with empirical difficulty. To reduce this confounding, SRCoD introduces a structural prior derived from intrinsic item structure. For each item j = ( v j , t j , y j ) j=(v_{j},t_{j},y_{j}) , we estimate a sample-wise multimodal interaction vector using the Lightweight Sample-wise Multimodal Interaction (LSMI) estimator [ 14 ] . We evaluate on three widely used vision-language benchmarks: ScienceQA [ 4 ] , MMMU [ 5 ] , and SEED-Bench [ 6 ] . They cover science-oriented question answering, college-level multimodal reasoning, and general multimodal understanding, respectively. Evaluation settings. We validate benchmark diagnosis methods under two complementary protocols. First, benchmark-refinement oriented validation follows the contaminated candidate-pool setting of prior work [ 18 ] : each pool contains both clean benchmark items and synthetic low-quality items generated by swapping image or text components across questions. A method selects a compact subset from this pool, and the subset is evaluated by how well it preserves the model ranking induced by the full clean benchmark. Second, human-labeled item validation evaluates whether a method recovers the dominant evidence factor of each item. We construct a human-labeled diagnostic validation set from ScienceQA, MMMU, and SEED-Bench. Candidate items are first filtered under the original full multimodal condition to ensure human solvability, and each retained item is then annotated under controlled evidence conditions. This yields a human evidence-sufficiency reference in a four-factor diagnostic space: Redundant, Visual-dominant, Textual-dominant, or Synergistic. The validation set contains 1,000 items per benchmark and is used only for evaluation. For quantitative evaluation, we compare each method’s dominant diagnostic factor with the human reference and report accuracy and macro-F1. Full annotation details are provided in Appendix C . Model pool and response collection. For methods using extrinsic responses, we collect modality-conditioned responses from a heterogeneous pool of VLMs, including proprietary and open-weight models from GPT-series [ 20 ] , Qwen-VL [ 21 ] , Gemma [ 22 ] , Ministral [ 23 ] , and other model families. The full model list, prompts, and implementation details are provided in Appendix D . Compared methods. We compare SRCoD with six baselines in total. Random selects a diagnostic factor uniformly at random. Raw directly maps modality-conditioned correctness gaps to the four diagnostic factors. LSMI [ 14 ] is a structure-only baseline that infers the dominant evidence factor from sample-wise multimodal interaction signals. IRT [ 16 ] is a standard psychometric baseline based on item difficulty, while MIRT [ 17 ] extends IRT with modality-conditioned response factors. M3IRT [ 18 ] is a stronger multimodal IRT baseline that models modality-specific item behavior from extrinsic responses. In contrast, SRCoD incorporates intrinsic structural signals as soft priors and infers the dominant evidence factor from its learned response-calibrated profile. 4.2 Main Results Benchmark-refinement oriented validation. We first conduct benchmark-refinement oriented validation to assess whether diagnostic scores can support reliable benchmark-based model comparison. In this setting, no item-level diagnostic labels are used. Instead, following the contaminated candidate-pool protocol of prior work [ 18 ] , we evaluate whether a diagnosis method can select compact subsets that preserve the model-ranking conclusions of the full clean benchmark. For each benchmark, we first compute a reference model ranking using the full clean set. We then construct a contaminated candidate pool by combining the clean items with an equal number of synthetic low-quality items. Following prior work [ 18 ] , the low-quality items are generated by swapping image or text components across different questions, producing shortcut-prone or unsolvable examples while preserving the benchmark format. The resulting candidate pool contains 50% clean items and 50% synthetic low-quality items. We compare Random selection, IRT, M3IRT, and SRCoD. For each method, we select subsets with sizes corresponding to 5 % 5\% , 10 % 10\% , 15 % 15\% , 20 % 20\% , and 25 % 25\% of the clean set size. The selected subset is then used to compute model accuracies and induce a subset-based model ranking. We measure ranking preservation by the Spearman rank correlation between this subset-induced ranking and the reference ranking obtained from the full clean benchmark: ρ = Spearman ⁡ ( rank clean , rank subset ) . \rho=\operatorname{Spearman}\left(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{clean}},\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{subset}}\right). (13) A higher ρ \rho indicates that the selected subset better preserves the evaluation conclusion of the full clean benchmark. For each subset size, we repeat item-pool resampling 20 times and report the mean and standard deviation of Spearman rank correlation. Figure 2 shows that SRCoD achieves strong benchmark-refinement oriented validation performance under contaminated candidate pools. On ScienceQA, SRCoD maintains high rank correlation across all subset sizes and is consistently stronger than IRT and Random, while remaining competitive with M3IRT. On MMMU, SRCoD achieves the best performance for subset sizes of 10 % 10\% and above, with rank correlation approaching the full clean benchmark ranking even with relatively small subsets. On SEED-Bench, SRCoD and M3IRT both perform strongly, but SRCoD reaches near-ceiling rank correlation from 10 % 10\% onward and remains substantially better than IRT and Random. Overall, these results indicate that the diagnostic profiles produced by SRCoD can identify items that preserve reliable model-comparison conclusions even when the candidate pool is contaminated. The comparison among baselines highlights the complementary roles of intrinsic item structure and extrinsic model responses. The structure-only LSMI baseline performs above random assignment in accuracy but obtains relatively low macro-F1, indicating that intrinsic structural signals capture some dominant dependence patterns but are insufficient for balanced diagnosis across all categories. The structural prior preserves intrinsic modality-dependence information, while response-side calibration adjusts this prior using observed modality-conditioned responses. This example demonstrates that SRCoD provides an interpretable diagnostic result by identifying how the available evidence contributes to answerability. 5 Conclusion This paper studied item-level multimodal benchmark diagnosis. We proposed SRCoD, a structure-anchored multimodal IRT framework that co-calibrates intrinsic item structure with extrinsic model responses. By using sample-wise multimodal interaction signals as structural priors and calibrating them with modality-conditioned response behavior, SRCoD produces fine-grained diagnostic profiles for redundant, visual-dominant, textual-dominant, and synergistic items. We also introduced a controlled human validation protocol and constructed a diagnostic validation set across ScienceQA, MMMU, and SEED-Bench. Experiments show that SRCoD outperforms intrinsic-structure and extrinsic-response baselines in item-level diagnosis, remains more stable under limited model pools, and preserves model rankings when selecting compact benchmark subsets. Future work may extend this framework to open-ended tasks and broader multimodal settings beyond vision and language.
